title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) guidance: defining service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning methodology, reliability initiatives, standards for incident reviews and postmortems, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended for SREs, service owners, and product/engineering teams responsible for production LLM inference services.

Goals
- Provide a single source of truth for SLO and error budget policy.
- Standardize capacity planning to ensure predictable latency and throughput for hosted and dedicated deployments.
- Define incident review and postmortem expectations to drive measurable reliability improvements.
- Catalog tooling and provide runnable runbooks for common operational scenarios.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles
- SLOs express user-facing expectations (latency, availability, correctness) for a single customer-visible metric.
- Keep SLOs simple: one objective per SLO.
- Assign clear owners (service owner and SRE partner).
- Use error budgets to allow safe risk-taking (deployments, experiments) while protecting customer experience.

Required SLOs (applies to inference-hosting services)
- Availability SLO: successful-response rate >= 99.95% over a 30-day rolling window. Measured as 2xx or 4xx responses for valid client requests; 5xx and 429 are considered failures unless explicitly accepted as degraded mode.
- P50/P95/P99 latency SLOs (inference request end-to-end): P95 <= 120ms, P99 <= 350ms for small models (<= 8k context); P95 <= 250ms, P99 <= 700ms for large models (> 8k context).
- Cold-start SLO: 99% of cold-starts complete within 5s for supported dedicated pools.
- Correctness SLO (where applicable): pass rate on critical prompt tests >= 98% per release (see quality-guardrails doc).

Error budget policy
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. For availability 99.95% => error budget = 0.05% over the SLO window.
- Track consumption continuously and publish dashboards: 30-day burn rate, 7-day burn rate, and projected exhaustion date.
- Thresholds and actions:
  1. Advisory (burn rate > 2x projected): notify service owner and SRE. Investigate cause; pause low-risk experiments.
  2. Restricted (burn rate > 5x): freeze non-critical rollouts and major config changes, escalate to platform lead.
  3. Emergency (burn rate > 10x or projected exhaustion < 24h): call incident, follow critical incident runbook.
- Use error budget for: canary rollouts, experimental model swaps, capacity burst tests. Document all uses in the change log.

SLO ownership and review cadence
- Owner: product/service owner (primary) and SRE (secondary).
- Quarterly SLO review with metrics, incident correlation, and proposal for adjustments.
- SLO change process: proposal -> SRE review -> stakeholder signoff -> update monitoring/alerting -> communicate to customers if change affects SLA.

2) Capacity Planning

High-level approach
- Two planning horizons: tactical (1-8 weeks) and strategic (6-18 months).
- Separate capacity for Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments. Hosted API must maintain regional headroom for traffic spikes and failovers.
- Inputs: historical traffic (RPS, token/sec), model mix (model families, quantization), sequence length distribution, duty cycle by time-of-day, and known upcoming events (sales, launches).

Capacity model (summary table)
- Example (text table):
  | Resource           | Target headroom | Measurement window | Owner | Notes |
  |--------------------|-----------------|--------------------|-------|-------|
  | GPU capacity (A100) | 20% peak headroom | 7d rolling peak    | SRE-Fleet | support autoscale and burst pools |
  | Inference quota (requests/sec) | 25% buffer for bursts | 1h peak | Platform | reserve for marketplace spikes |
  | Network egress | 30% buffer | 24h peak | Infra | monitor multi-region egress |

Tactical planning steps (1-8 weeks)
1. Weekly capacity review: present 7d rolling demand, current utilization, and any projected launches.
2. If projected utilization > 70% of reserved capacity sustained for 24h, open capacity expansion RFC and schedule procurement or reallocation.
3. Validate autoscaler policies: target utilization, cooldowns, and burst behavior against synthetic traffic.
4. Prepare mitigation playbook for capacity shortage (flow control, degrade non-critical workloads, switch to alternative model variants).

Strategic planning (6-18 months)
- Maintain a capacity forecast by region and by model family; incorporate expected model onboarding and major customer commitments (Dedicated contracts).
- Track gross margin per-token for each model family to prioritize resource allocation.
- Quarterly review with finance and product to book reserved capacity and procurement cycles.

Capacity testing and validation
- Monthly load tests on a staging fleet with a production-like model mix and sequence-length distribution.
- Chaos tests for region failure and simulated cold-start storms.
- Document test results and post-test corrective actions in the capacity runbook.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

Program structure
- Reliability initiatives are tracked as epics in the engineering roadmap and must include: success metrics (SLO delta, reduced incident MTTR), owner, timeline, and rollout plan.
- Prioritization criteria: customer impact (error budget burn), cost-to-fix, recurrence frequency, and ease of automation.

Common initiative examples
- Prefix/KV cache warmup for common request patterns to reduce P99 latency by 30%.
- Smart batching improvements to increase throughput by 20% at equivalent latency.
- Improved observability for model swap metrics (latency by model variant, rejection rates).

Measuring success
- Define success criteria before the work starts (e.g., reduce P99 by 40ms under 95th-percentile load).
- Post-rollout verification: 14-day monitoring window and compare to baseline.

4) Incident Review Standards and Postmortems

Incident classification
- SEV0 / SEV1: major outages with customer-visible impact across multiple customers or regions.
- SEV2: partial service degradation affecting a subset of tenants or models.
- SEV3: localized degradation, non-urgent, or internal-only issues.

Postmortem requirements (all SEV1/SEV0 required; SEV2 at SRE discretion)
- Template fields (must be present):
  - Incident ID
  - Timeline (UTC timestamps)
  - Summary (one-paragraph customer-facing description)
  - Impact (metrics: % availability drop, number of affected customers, SLO burn)
  - Root cause analysis (RCA) with evidence and hypothesis verification steps
  - Corrective actions (short-term mitigations and longer-term fixes)
  - Action owner and due date for each corrective action
  - Postmortem review date and attendees
  - Follow-up verification plan and metrics

Postmortem process
1. Produce a draft within 72 hours of incident mitigation.
2. Complete RCA and action list within 7 days.
3. Review session within 10 business days with engineering, product, SRE, and customer success if customers affected.
4. Publish final postmortem to Confluence and link to the incident timeline in status page.
5. Track action items in the engineering issue tracker and require closure or re-assignment for any overdue items after 30 days.

Blameless review culture
- Focus on systemic causes, not individual errors. Use "why" repeatedly to move from human error to process or tooling gaps.
- When human error contributed, document improved guardrails (pre-merge checks, automation) as corrective actions.

5) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

Core toolset (examples)
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term retention.
- Dashboards & alerting: Grafana (service dashboards, SLO burn, capacity alarms).
- Tracing: Jaeger / OpenTelemetry for distributed inference traces (API gateway -> routing -> runtime).
- Logging: Loki / ELK for structured request and runtime logs; request IDs must be present on all logs.
- On-call and Escalation: PagerDuty for paging; Slack incident channels for coordination.
- Incident timeline: Incident.io or equivalent for live incident timelines and roles.
- Runbook execution: Internal runbook runner (CLI tool) that supports templated commands and checklists.

Standard dashboards and alerts
- SLO Burn Dashboard: 30-day/7-day burn rate panels, projected exhaustion time.
- Capacity Health: utilization by region and model family, autoscaler event frequency, queued requests.
- Runtime Health: GPU memory pressure, NVLink errors, kernel retry rates, cold-start frequency.
- Incidents: active incidents list, severity, timeline link, assigned owners.

Alerting policy
- Alert noise reduction is critical: alerts must map to an action in a runbook and have a clear owner.
- Alert severity mapping: P1 (page immediately), P2 (notify Slack and on-call), P3 (ticket only).
- All P1 alerts must include a playbook link and expected first-action time in description.

6) Canonical SRE Runbooks (examples)

A. High error-rate (5xx) on hosted API
- Symptoms: sustained 5xx rate > 0.5% for 5 minutes and SLO burn rate > 2x.
- Immediate actions:
  1. PagerDuty page to on-call.
  2. Check Grafana SLO Burn dashboard and request logs for surge patterns.
  3. Confirm if a recent deployment or model swap occurred; if so, rollback canary.
  4. If backend runtime OOM or kernel errors are present, switch traffic to warmed alternate pool.
  5. Notify product and CS for customer-impacted routes.
- Mitigation checklist:
  - Enable traffic shedding for non-critical tenants.
  - Increase instance count in autoscaler if safe and capacity allows.
  - Re-route to secondary region if primary region impacted.

B. Elevated P99 latency for a model variant
- Symptoms: P99 increased by > 2x baseline for 10 minutes.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Identify affected model variant and cohort via model-swap metrics in Grafana.
  2. Check KV cache hit rates and cold-start counts.
  3. If warm caches are low, trigger targeted cache warmups for top prefixes.
  4. If specific kernel regression is suspected, roll back kernel or switch to compatible runtime.
  5. Throttle low-priority workloads and route premium traffic to unaffected variants.

C. Capacity shortage (GPU util > 90% sustained)
- Symptoms: sustained GPU utilization > 90% for > 30 minutes and queueing observed.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Notify SRE-Fleet and open a capacity incident.
  2. Trigger autoscaler emergency policy to add burst nodes.
  3. Deprioritize batch jobs and non-critical experiments.
  4. Temporarily reduce sampling or lower default token limits for non-paid tiers.

Runbook templates
- Each runbook must include: Preconditions, Detection criteria, Immediate actions, Rollback steps, Communication checklist, Post-incident actions, Link to related runbooks.

7) Verification and Continuous Improvement

- Quarterly reliability review: aggregate incident metrics, trend SLO health, and update priority initiatives.
- Runbook drills: monthly tabletop exercises and quarterly live drills for critical runbooks (regional failover, cold-start storm).
- Internal SLA & SLO training for new engineers: onboarding module with exercises on reading SLO dashboards and executing a runbook.

Appendices
A. SLO measurement definitions
- Request success criteria: HTTP 2xx and valid domain-specific 4xx. Client-side timeouts and cancelled requests excluded from availability calculations unless they reflect server-side delay.
- Latency measurement window: API response time measured at API gateway ingress to final token emission acknowledgment. Percentiles must be computed using a high-resolution histogram (e.g., HDRHistogram) with 1ms buckets.

B. Example alerts
- SLO burn high: Alert when 7-day burn rate > 4 and projected exhaustion < 72 hours. Pager duty: P1. Playbook: link to SLO burn runbook.
- GPU ECC errors: Alert on > 3 ECC events/min on any host. Pager duty: P1. Owner: SRE-Fleet.

C. Contacts and ownership
- SRE on-call rotation: see internal on-call schedule link.
- SRE-Fleet owners: Diego Ramos (diego@redwood.ai)
- Platform SRE lead: Maya Patel (maya@redwood.ai)
- Incident commander escalation: Head of SRE (Sofia Nguyen)

Document maintenance
- Owner: SRE leadership (Owner team: engineering).
- Review cadence: quarterly for SLOs/capacity; runbooks reviewed after each major incident and at least annually.
- Change log: record key edits and rationale at the top of the Confluence page.
